  if a[i-1] > b[j]: take fewer from a; else take more
median from max(left parts) and min(right parts)
hints.walkthrough: Merging both lists is O(n + m). To do better, search for the dividing line of the merged order. If you take i numbers from the shorter list and j = half - i from the other for the left half, the split is correct when every left number is <= every right number; since each list is already sorted that only needs a[i-1] <= b[j] and b[j-1] <= a[i]. If a[i-1] > b[j] you took too many from a (decrease i); otherwise take more. Treat missing elements as minus and plus infinity at the ends. When a valid split is found, the median comes from the largest left value (odd total) or the average of the largest left and smallest right value (even total).

problems.title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
problems.statement:
Two shelves hold books numbered in increasing order: `first` and `second` (both sorted from smallest to largest, either may be empty but not both).

Return **one sorted list** containing all the numbers from both.
constraints: 0 <= len(first), len(second) <= 100000, and at least one is not empty
-1000000000 <= values <= 1000000000, each list sorted in non-decreasing order

examples.explanation: Take the smaller front number each time.
One shelf is empty.

hints.nudge: Both lists are already sorted. Where is the smallest remaining number?
hints.pattern: Two pointers, one per list, always taking the smaller front value.
hints.pseudocode:
i = 0; j = 0; result = []
while i < n and j < m:
  if first[i] <= second[j]: append first[i]; i++ else: append second[j]; j++
append the rest of whichever list is left
hints.walkthrough: Concatenating and sorting costs O((n+m) log(n+m)) and ignores that the lists are sorted. Instead compare the two front elements, take the smaller, and advance that list's pointer. When one list runs out, copy what remains of the other. Every element is handled once: O(n + m). This is the 'merge' step of merge sort.

problems.title: Merge Two Linked Lists
problems.statement:
You are given `first` and `second`, the heads of two singly linked lists, each **sorted from smallest to largest**. Either list may be empty.

Merge them into **one sorted linked list** by splicing the nodes together, and return its head. (In the examples each list is shown as the list of its values.)
constraints: 0 <= number of nodes in each list <= 50000
-1000000000 <= node value <= 1000000000, each list sorted in non-decreasing order

examples.explanation: Take the smaller front value each time.
Two empty lists merge into an empty list.

hints.nudge: Compare the two front nodes. Which one comes first in the merged list?
hints.pattern: Two pointers plus a dummy head node, linking the smaller node each time.
hints.pseudocode:
dummy = new node; tail = dummy
while first and second:
  if first.val <= second.val: tail.next = first; first = first.next
  else: tail.next = second; second = second.next
  tail = tail.next
tail.next = first or second
return dummy.next
hints.walkthrough: Pick the smaller of the two front nodes, attach it to the end of the result, and advance in that list. A temporary 'dummy' node at the start avoids special cases for the first node. When one list runs out, attach the remaining nodes of the other list in one step (they are already sorted). Nodes are re-linked, not copied: O(1) extra space and O(n + m) time.

problems.title: Middle of the List
problems.statement:
You are given `head`, the first node of a singly linked list with at least one node.

Return the **value of the middle node**. If the list has an even number of nodes there are two middle nodes: return the value of the **second** one. (In the examples the list is shown as the list of its values.)

examples.explanation: The middle of five nodes is the third.
Two middles (3 and 4): return the second.

hints.nudge: A list has no index, so you cannot jump to the middle. What if one pointer walked twice as fast as another?
hints.pattern: Slow and fast pointers.
hints.pseudocode:
slow = head; fast = head
while fast and fast.next:
  slow = slow.next; fast = fast.next.next
return slow.val
hints.walkthrough: You could count the nodes and walk n/2 steps (two passes). A single pass uses two pointers: slow moves one node at a time, fast moves two. When fast reaches the end, slow has covered half the distance, so it stands on the middle. For an even number of nodes the loop ends one step later, leaving slow on the second middle, exactly what the problem asks.

problems.title: Fewest Coins
problems.statement:
A vending machine has coins of the values in `coins`, and you have an unlimited number of each value. Return the **fewest coins** needed to make exactly `amount`.

If the amount cannot be made, return `-1`. The amount `0` needs `0` coins.

examples.explanation: No combination of 4s and 6s adds up to 7.

hints.nudge: Suppose you already knew the fewest coins for every smaller amount. How would you get the answer for this amount?
hints.pattern: Dynamic programming over amounts: best[a] = 1 + min(best[a - coin]) over all coins.
hints.walkthrough: A greedy choice (always the biggest coin) can fail: with coins 1, 3, 4 and amount 6, greedy takes 4+1+1 (3 coins) but 3+3 uses 2. Plain recursion trying every coin is exponential. Instead fill a table best[a] = fewest coins for amount a, from 0 upward: the last coin used was some c, so best[a] = 1 + best[a - c] for the best c. Amounts that cannot be made stay at infinity. The answer is best[amount], or -1 if it is infinity. O(n * amount) time.

problems.title: Cheapest Route
problems.statement:
A country has `n` cities numbered `0` to `n - 1` and **one-way** roads. Each entry `roads[i] = [from, to, cost]` is a road from city `from` to city `to` that costs `cost` (always positive) to use.

Return the **smallest total cost** of a trip from city `start` to city `end`, or `-1` if the trip is impossible. A trip from a city to itself costs `0`.

examples.explanation: 0 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3 costs 1 + 2 + 1 = 4, cheaper than 0 -> 2 -> 3 which costs 6.
The only road goes from 0 to 1, not back.

hints.nudge: Always expanding the city with the smallest known cost so far guarantees you never find a cheaper way to it later. Why does that need positive costs?
hints.pattern: Dijkstra's algorithm with a priority queue (min-heap).
hints.pseudocode:
dist[start] = 0; heap = [(0, start)]
while heap: (d, u) = pop smallest
  if d > dist[u]: continue
  if u == end: return d
  for each road (u -> v, w): if d + w < dist[v]: dist[v] = d + w; push (d + w, v)
return -1
hints.walkthrough: Breadth-first search counts roads, not costs, so it fails here. Dijkstra keeps the best known cost to each city and always expands the cheapest unfinished city (a min-heap gives it in O(log n)). Because every cost is positive, the first time a city is taken from the heap its cost is final. Skip stale heap entries (d larger than the stored distance). When the end city is taken, return its cost; if the heap empties first, the end is unreachable. Bellman-Ford (relax every road n - 1 times) also works in O(n * m).

problems.title: Cheapest Way Up the Stairs
problems.statement:
A staircase has steps numbered from 0, and `cost[i]` is the price you pay **when you step on step `i`**. After paying you may climb **one or two steps**. You may start on step 0 or on step 1. The top of the staircase is one step past the last step (arriving there costs nothing).

Return the **minimum total price** to reach the top.

examples.explanation: Start on step 1 (pay 15), then climb two steps to the top.
Step on steps 0, 2, 4, 6, 7 and 9 (each costs 1) and skip all three steps that cost 100: total 6.

hints.nudge: To be about to step on step i, you came from step i-1 (and paid for it) or from step i-2 (and paid for it). Which is cheaper?
hints.pattern: Dynamic programming over positions: best(i) = min(best(i-1) + cost[i-1], best(i-2) + cost[i-2]).
hints.pseudocode:
prev2 = 0; prev1 = 0      // best(0) and best(1): you may start on step 0 or 1 for free
for i from 2 to n:
  current = min(prev1 + cost[i-1], prev2 + cost[i-2])
  prev2 = prev1; prev1 = current
return prev1              // best(n) = the top
hints.walkthrough: Let best(i) be the cheapest total to be standing at position i, meaning 'about to step on step i'. Positions 0 and 1 cost nothing because you may start on either step. To reach position i you came from position i-1 by paying cost[i-1], or from position i-2 by paying cost[i-2], so best(i) = min of those two. The answer is best(n), the top. Plain recursion tries every route (exponential); a table, or just the last two values, does it in O(n).

problems.title: Fewest Jumps to the End
problems.statement:
You stand on the first square of a row of squares. `jumps[i]` is the **maximum** number of squares you can jump forward from square `i` (any shorter distance is allowed too). The last square can always be reached.

Return the **minimum number of jumps** needed to get from the first square to the last one. If there is only one square the answer is `0`.
constraints: the last square is always reachable

examples.explanation: Jump 1 step (to index 1), then 3 steps to the last square.
Same idea: 0 -> 1 -> 4.

hints.nudge: Think in 'rounds': after 1 jump you can be anywhere in some range; after 2 jumps in a bigger range...
hints.pattern: Greedy / BFS by levels: track the end of the range reachable with the current number of jumps, and the farthest you could get with one more.
hints.pseudocode:
jumps_used = 0; range_end = 0; farthest = 0
for i in 0..n-2:
  farthest = max(farthest, i + jumps[i])
  if i == range_end: jumps_used++; range_end = farthest
return jumps_used
hints.walkthrough: A table of the fewest jumps to every square costs O(n^2). Instead process the squares in 'rounds'. All squares reachable with k jumps form a range ending at range_end. While scanning that range, record the farthest square any of them can reach (farthest). When you pass the end of the current range you must take one more jump, and the new range ends at farthest. Count how many times this happens before reaching the last square. One pass: O(n) time, O(1) space.

problems.title: Smallest in a Rotated List
problems.statement:
A list of **different** numbers was sorted from smallest to largest and then **rotated** (cut at some position, with the two parts swapped), so `[0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7]` can become `[4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2]`. It may also be left unrotated.

Return the **smallest number** in `nums`.
constraints: nums is a sorted list that was rotated by some amount

examples.explanation: The list was [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] rotated.
Not rotated: the first value is the smallest.

hints.nudge: Compare the middle element with the last one. What does it tell you about where the smallest number is?
hints.pattern: Binary search toward the rotation point.
hints.pseudocode:
lo = 0; hi = n - 1
while lo < hi:
  mid = (lo + hi) / 2
  if nums[mid] > nums[hi]: lo = mid + 1   // the drop is to the right of mid
  else: hi = mid                           // mid could be the smallest
return nums[lo]
hints.walkthrough: Taking the minimum of everything is O(n). The smallest value sits right after the 'drop' where the list falls from a large number to a small one. If nums[mid] is greater than nums[hi], the drop is somewhere to the right of mid, so the minimum is in (mid, hi]. Otherwise the part from mid to hi is sorted, so the minimum is at mid or to its left. Narrow the range until one element is left.

problems.title: Shortest Stretch to Reach a Total
problems.statement:
Every day a savings jar receives the amount `deposits[i]` (always positive). You want to reach at least `target` coins using a **stretch of consecutive days**.

Return the **fewest days** in a stretch whose deposits add up to **at least** `target`, or `0` if no stretch is enough.

examples.explanation: The days 4 and 3 add up to 7.
All the deposits together are only 3.

hints.nudge: Because deposits are positive, adding a day only increases the total and removing a day only decreases it.
hints.pattern: Two pointers: grow the right end until you reach the target, then shrink the left end as long as you still do.
hints.pseudocode:
left = 0; sum = 0; best = infinity
for right in 0..n-1:
  sum += deposits[right]
  while sum >= target: best = min(best, right - left + 1); sum -= deposits[left]; left++
return best or 0
hints.walkthrough: Checking every start and end is O(n^2). With positive numbers you can use a sliding window: extend the right end until the sum reaches the target, then record the length and move the left end forward while the sum still reaches the target (each move can only shorten the window). Both pointers only move forward, so O(n) total. If best was never updated return 0.

problems.title: Smallest Covering Window
problems.statement:
You have a long `text` and a short word `need`. A **window** is a stretch of consecutive letters of `text`. A window **covers** `need` if it contains every letter of `need`, as many times as that letter appears in `need` (extra letters in the window are fine).

Return the **length of the shortest window that covers `need`**, or `0` if no window does.
constraints: both strings contain only lowercase letters a-z

examples.explanation: The window banc contains a, b and c.
The text has only one a, but two are needed.

hints.nudge: Grow a window to the right until it covers `need`. Then, how can you make it smaller without breaking it?
hints.pattern: Sliding window with letter counts: expand the right end, then shrink the left end while the window still covers.
hints.walkthrough: Checking every window is O(n^2) windows times a check. Use two pointers. Keep a table of how many of each letter are still needed (it can go negative for extras) and a counter 'missing' of letters not yet covered. Move right one letter at a time. Whenever missing reaches 0 the window covers need: record its length, then move left forward to try to shrink it (if you remove a letter that was needed, missing goes up again and you stop shrinking). Each pointer moves at most n times, so O(n).

problems.title: Missing Number
problems.statement:
A box should contain tickets numbered `0, 1, 2, ..., n`, but one ticket is lost, so only `n` tickets are left in `numbers`, all different.

Return the **number of the lost ticket**.
constraints: numbers contains n different values taken from 0..n, where n = len(numbers)

examples.explanation: The tickets 0..3 should all be there; 2 is missing.
0 and 1 are present, so the lost ticket is the last one, 2.

hints.nudge: You know exactly which numbers should be there. What is their total?
hints.pattern: Compare an expected total with the actual total.
hints.pseudocode:
expected = n * (n + 1) / 2
return expected - sum(numbers)
hints.walkthrough: Checking each possible ticket against the whole list is O(n^2). The numbers 0..n add up to n*(n+1)/2. The list contains all of them except one, so the missing ticket is the expected total minus the actual total of the list. One pass, O(1) extra space.

problems.title: Find the Peak
problems.statement:
`heights` describes a mountain trail: the heights **strictly increase up to one peak and then strictly decrease** (so there are at least 3 values, and the peak is never the first or last one).

Return the **index of the peak**.
constraints: heights strictly increases and then strictly decreases

examples.explanation: 2 is the highest and sits at index 1.
The peak is 10.

hints.nudge: Look at the middle element and the one after it. Are you going uphill or downhill there?
hints.pattern: Binary search on the slope: compare heights[mid] with heights[mid + 1].
hints.pseudocode:
lo = 0; hi = n - 1
while lo < hi:
  mid = (lo + hi) / 2
  if heights[mid] < heights[mid + 1]: lo = mid + 1   // still climbing: peak is to the right
  else: hi = mid                                      // descending: peak is at mid or to the left
return lo
hints.walkthrough: A scan for the maximum is O(n). On this trail, if heights[mid] < heights[mid + 1] you are on the way up, so the peak is to the right of mid. Otherwise you are on the way down (or at the peak), so the peak is at mid or to its left. Keep shrinking the range; when it has one element left, that is the peak. O(log n).

problems.title: Peaceful Queens
problems.statement:
On an `n` by `n` chessboard you want to place `n` queens so that **no two queens attack each other**. A queen attacks every square in its own row, its own column, and along both diagonals.

Return the **number of different ways** to place the `n` queens.

examples.explanation: A 4 x 4 board has exactly two peaceful arrangements (mirror images of each other).
One queen on a 1 x 1 board.

hints.nudge: There must be exactly one queen in each row. So place them row by row. For each row, which columns are still safe?
hints.pattern: Backtracking: place a queen in the next row in any safe column, recurse, then undo.
hints.pseudocode:
place(row): if row == n: return 1
  total = 0
  for each column c that is not attacked (column, diagonal, anti-diagonal unused):
    mark c; total += place(row + 1); unmark c
  return total
hints.walkthrough: Trying every placement of n queens on n*n squares is hopeless, but one queen per row is forced, so place queens row by row. In each row try every column, skipping those attacked by the queens already placed: same column, same diagonal (row - col equal) or same anti-diagonal (row + col equal). Keep three sets (or bit masks) of used columns and diagonals so each check is O(1). When all n rows are filled, count one solution; then undo the last queen and try the next column (backtracking). The counts for n = 1..9 are 1, 0, 0, 2, 10, 4, 40, 92, 352.

problems.title: Nearby Duplicate
problems.statement:
A camera logs a number each second in `readings`. A repeat is **suspicious** if the same number appears at two different positions that are at most `k` apart.

Return `true` if there are two positions `i != j` with `readings[i] == readings[j]` and `|i - j| <= k`, otherwise `false`.

examples.explanation: The 1s are at positions 0 and 3, which are 3 apart.
Equal numbers are always 3 apart, which is more than 2.

hints.nudge: When you see a number, what single piece of information about its last appearance is enough?
hints.pattern: Hash map from value to its most recent index.
hints.walkthrough: Comparing every pair within distance k costs O(n*k). Scan once and remember, for each value, the index where you last saw it. If the current value was seen before and the gap i - last is at most k, you found a suspicious repeat. Otherwise update the last index to i (only the closest earlier copy matters). O(n) time.

problems.title: Next Arrangement
problems.statement:
Think of all the different ways to arrange the numbers of `nums`, listed in dictionary order (compare the first numbers, then the second, and so on). Return the arrangement that comes **right after** `nums` in that list.

If `nums` is already the last arrangement (the numbers are in descending order), wrap around and return the **first** arrangement (ascending order). The list can contain repeated numbers.

examples.explanation: After 1 2 3 comes 1 3 2.
3 2 1 is the last arrangement, so wrap around to the smallest.

hints.nudge: To get the NEXT arrangement you change as little as possible, so you change a digit as far to the right as you can.
hints.pattern: Find the last place where the sequence goes up, swap with the next larger value on its right, then reverse the tail.
hints.pseudocode:
i = n-2; while i >= 0 and nums[i] >= nums[i+1]: i--
if i >= 0:
  j = n-1; while nums[j] <= nums[i]: j--
  swap(nums[i], nums[j])
reverse(nums[i+1 .. n-1])
hints.walkthrough: Scan from the right for the first index i where nums[i] < nums[i+1]. Everything to the right of i is in descending order, i.e. already the largest possible arrangement of those numbers, so to go to the next arrangement you must increase position i. Choose the smallest number on the right that is still bigger than nums[i] (the rightmost one that is > nums[i], because the tail is descending), swap it with nums[i], then reverse the tail so it becomes the smallest possible (ascending). If no such i exists, the whole list is descending: reversing it gives the first arrangement.

problems.title: Binary Strings Without Twin Ones
problems.statement:
A binary string is made of the characters `0` and `1`. Count the binary strings of length exactly `n` that **never have two `1`s next to each other** (for example `0101` is fine, `0110` is not).

Return the number of such strings.

examples.explanation: 00, 01 and 10 (11 is not allowed).

hints.nudge: Build the string one character at a time. What does the last character you wrote decide about the next one?
hints.pattern: Backtracking: append 0 always, append 1 only when the last character is not 1. Then notice the same states repeat.
hints.pseudocode:
count(remaining, lastWasOne):
  if remaining == 0: return 1
  total = count(remaining - 1, false)          // put a 0
  if not lastWasOne: total += count(remaining - 1, true)   // put a 1
  return total
hints.walkthrough: Checking all 2^n strings works for small n only. Building the string character by character is faster because you never extend a string that already has two adjacent ones: a 0 can always be added, a 1 only after a 0 (or at the start). The number of completions depends only on how many characters remain and whether the last one was a 1, so remember those answers (memoization) or keep two running counts: strings ending in 0 and strings ending in 1. Each step: new_zero = zero + one, new_one = zero. The answer for n = 30 is 2178309.

problems.title: Paint the Fence
problems.statement:
A fence has `posts` posts in a row and you have `colors` colors of paint. Every post gets exactly one color. The rule: **no three posts in a row may have the same color** (two in a row is fine).

Return the **number of different ways** to paint the fence.

examples.explanation: With 2 colors there are 8 ways to paint 3 posts, minus the 2 ways that use one color on all three.
Any pair of colors is allowed: 3 * 3.

hints.nudge: Look at the last two posts. Are they the same color or different? That decides what the next post may be.
hints.pattern: Dynamic programming with two counts: ways where the last two posts match, and ways where they differ.
hints.pseudocode:
same = colors; diff = colors * (colors - 1)      // after 2 posts
repeat posts - 2 times: (same, diff) = (diff, (same + diff) * (colors - 1))
return same + diff    // for posts == 1 the answer is just colors
hints.walkthrough: Count paintings by whether the last two posts have the same color. A new post can always get a color different from the previous post: (colors - 1) choices, from any painting. It can copy the previous post's color only if the previous two posts were different. So new_same = diff, new_diff = (same + diff) * (colors - 1). Start after two posts with same = colors and diff = colors * (colors - 1), and handle posts = 1 separately (the answer is colors). O(n) time. Checking all colors^posts paintings is only fine for tiny fences.

problems.title: Pair Count
problems.statement:
A shop has `prices`. A customer wants to buy exactly two different items whose prices add up to exactly `budget`.

Count how many pairs of positions `(i, j)` with `i < j` satisfy `prices[i] + prices[j] == budget`. Two items with the same price at different positions count as different pairs.

examples.explanation: The pairs are (2,4), (3,3) and (1,5).
Any two of the four items work: 4 choose 2 = 6.

hints.nudge: For one price p, which exact price would complete the pair? How could you check that quickly?
hints.pattern: Hash map of counts: how many times each price has appeared so far.
hints.pseudocode:
count = {}; total = 0
for each p in prices:
  total = total + count.get(budget - p, 0)
  count[p] = count.get(p, 0) + 1
return total
hints.walkthrough: Checking every pair is O(n^2), too slow for 50,000 items. Scan left to right keeping a map from price to how many times you have seen it. For the current price p, every earlier item priced budget - p forms a valid pair with it, so add that count to the total. Then record p. Each pair is counted exactly once, when its second item is reached. O(n) time, O(n) space. The result can be over a billion, but fits in a 32-bit int for n <= 50,000.

problems.title: Palindrome Cuts
problems.statement:
Cut the string `text` into **pieces of consecutive letters** (the pieces together must give back the whole text, in order). A cutting is **good** if **every piece is a palindrome** (reads the same forwards and backwards). For example `aab` can be cut as `a|a|b` or `aa|b`, both good.

Return the **number of good cuttings**.
constraints: text contains only lowercase letters a-z

examples.explanation: a|a|b and aa|b.
a|a|a, a|aa, aa|a, aaa.

hints.nudge: Choose where the first piece ends. It must be a palindrome. What is left to cut afterwards?
hints.pattern: Backtracking over the end of the next piece; or dynamic programming over prefixes.
hints.walkthrough: Recursive version: from a start position, try every end position; if the piece is a palindrome, count the good cuttings of the rest. That recomputes the same suffixes, but with n <= 16 it is still fast. A faster idea: let ways[i] be the number of good cuttings of the first i letters. The last piece covers letters start..i-1; if it is a palindrome, it adds ways[start]. So ways[i] = sum of ways[start] over palindromic pieces ending at i. O(n^2) pieces, each checked in O(n).

problems.title: Split Into Equal Groups
problems.statement:
You are given a list of positive numbers `nums` and a number `k`. Can you divide **all** the numbers into exactly `k` groups (every number goes into exactly one group, and no group is empty) so that **every group has the same sum**?

Return `true` if it is possible, otherwise `false`.

examples.explanation: The total is 10, which cannot be split into 3 equal sums.

expected.time: O(k^n) worst case, fast with pruning

hints.nudge: If the groups are equal, what must each group's sum be? When is that impossible right away?
hints.pattern: Backtracking: put each number into a group that still has room, undo if it leads nowhere. Prune a lot.
hints.pseudocode:
total = sum(nums); if total % k != 0: return false; target = total / k
sort nums from largest to smallest; if the largest > target: return false
place(i): if i == n: return true
  for each group g (skip a group whose current sum was already tried for this number):
    if group[g] + nums[i] <= target: add; if place(i + 1): return true; undo
  return false
hints.walkthrough: First rule out the easy cases: the total must be divisible by k, and no number may exceed the target sum total / k. Then place the numbers one by one into k groups. Placing the biggest numbers first makes failures show up early. Never put a number into a group that would exceed the target. If two groups currently have the same sum, trying the second one is pointless (it leads to the same situation), so skip it. If every number gets placed, all groups end exactly at the target. A bitmask DP over subsets (2^n states) is another way.

problems.title: Peak Altitude
problems.statement:
A hiker starts a trail at altitude `0`. The trail is split into segments, and `changes[i]` is the net altitude change over segment `i` (positive = climbing, negative = descending).

Return the **highest altitude** the hiker reaches at any point, including the starting altitude `0`.

examples.explanation: Altitudes are 0, -5, -4, 1, 1, -6. The highest is 1.
The hiker only goes down, so the start (0) is the peak.

hints.nudge: Where is the hiker after segment 1? After segment 2? Try writing the altitudes for the first example.
hints.pattern: This is a running total (prefix sum): keep adding each change to the current altitude.
hints.walkthrough: Start with height = 0 and best = 0 (the start counts). Walk through the list once, adding each change to height. After each step, if height is bigger than best, update best. One pass, no extra memory: O(n) time, O(1) space. Recomputing the sum from the start for every position also works but is O(n^2).

problems.title: Peak Overlap
problems.statement:
A conference hall hosts talks. `talks[i] = [start, end]` means talk `i` runs from time `start` up to, but **not including**, time `end`. So a talk ending at time `t` does not overlap a talk starting at time `t`.

Return the **largest number of talks running at the same moment**.
constraints: talks[i] has exactly two numbers [start, end]

examples.explanation: At time 2 and 3 two talks run. At time 4 the first has ended and two others run.
Each talk ends exactly when the next begins, so they never overlap.

hints.nudge: The number of running talks only changes when a talk starts or ends. What if you looked at those moments in order?
hints.pattern: Sort the start times and the end times separately, then sweep through them.
hints.walkthrough: Checking every start time against every talk is O(n^2). Instead, split the talks into two sorted lists: all start times and all end times. Sweep forward: when the next start is earlier than the earliest unfinished end, a talk begins, so the count goes up; otherwise a talk ends first, so the count goes down. Because a talk ending at time t frees the room for one starting at t, ends win ties (the check is 'start < end', not '<='). Track the maximum count seen. O(n log n) from the sorting.

problems.title: Postfix Calculator
problems.statement:
A calculator uses **postfix notation**: the operator comes after its two numbers. For example `3 4 +` means 3 + 4, and `2 3 4 * -` means 2 - (3 * 4).

The expression `expr` is a list of tokens separated by single spaces. A token is either a non-negative whole number or one of the operators `+`, `-`, `*`. The expression is always valid, and every intermediate result fits in a 32-bit integer.

Return the value of the expression.
constraints: tokens are separated by exactly one space; operators are + - *
the expression is valid and no value exceeds the 32-bit integer range

hints.nudge: When you read an operator, which two numbers does it use? Which numbers have you seen most recently?
hints.pattern: A stack of numbers: push numbers, pop two when you see an operator.
hints.walkthrough: Read the tokens left to right. A number is pushed onto the stack. An operator needs the two most recent numbers, which are on top of the stack: pop b (the right operand) then a (the left operand), compute a op b, and push the result back. Order matters for minus: it is a - b, not b - a. When the tokens run out, the single value left on the stack is the answer. O(n) time.

problems.title: Fast Power
problems.statement:
Compute `base` raised to the power `exp`, **modulo `m`** (the remainder after dividing by `m`). The exponent can be as large as a billion, so multiplying `base` by itself `exp` times is too slow.

Return `(base ^ exp) mod m`. Note that `base ^ 0 = 1`, and the remainder of 1 divided by 1 is 0.

examples.explanation: Anything to the power 0 is 1.

hints.nudge: x^10 can be made from x^5: how many multiplications does it take to go from x^5 to x^10?
hints.pattern: Divide and conquer on the exponent: x^e = (x^(e/2))^2, times x when e is odd.
hints.pseudocode:
power(e): if e == 0: return 1 % m
  half = power(e / 2)
  result = half * half % m
  if e is odd: result = result * (base % m) % m
  return result
hints.walkthrough: Repeated multiplication takes exp steps, up to a billion. Halving the exponent solves it in about 30 steps: compute x^(e/2) recursively, square it, and multiply by one more x if e is odd. Take the remainder after every multiplication so numbers never get large (every product is below m*m = 9 * 10^8, which fits in a 32-bit int). The base case e = 0 returns 1 mod m (which is 0 when m = 1).

problems.title: Product of the Others
problems.statement:
Given `nums`, build a new list `result` where `result[i]` is the **product of all the numbers in `nums` except `nums[i]`**.

Return `result`. Try to do it without dividing (the list can contain zeros).

examples.explanation: For index 0: 2 * 3 * 4 = 24, and so on.
The zero makes every product 0 except the one that skips it: (-1) * 1 * (-3) * 3 = 9.

hints.nudge: result[i] is the product of everything to the left of i times the product of everything to the right of i.
hints.pattern: Prefix and suffix products.
hints.pseudocode:
left = 1
for i from 0 to n-1: result[i] = left; left *= nums[i]
right = 1
for i from n-1 down to 0: result[i] *= right; right *= nums[i]
hints.walkthrough: Multiplying all the others for every index costs O(n^2). Instead, make one pass from the left storing in result[i] the product of everything before i. Then make a pass from the right, multiplying result[i] by the product of everything after i. No division is needed, so zeros are handled automatically. O(n) time.

problems.title: Rain Catch
problems.statement:
A row of walls stands side by side, each one unit wide; `heights[i]` is the height of wall `i`. After a rainstorm, water collects in the gaps between walls.

A unit of water sits above wall `i` as long as there is a **taller-or-equal wall somewhere to its left AND somewhere to its right**; the water level there is the lower of the two best walls. Return the **total units of water** held by the whole row.

examples.explanation: Water fills the dips between the taller walls: 1 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 6 units.
The wide basin between the 4 and the 5 holds 9 units.

hints.nudge: How much water sits above one single wall? It depends on the tallest wall on each side.
hints.pattern: Two pointers moving inward, always handling the side with the lower wall.
hints.walkthrough: Above wall i the water level is min(tallest wall to the left, tallest wall to the right) and the water is that level minus h[i] (never below 0). Computing both maxima for every wall costs O(n^2). With two pointers you track the best wall seen from each end. Whichever end currently has the lower wall is the limiting side: its water level is decided by its own running maximum, because the other side is guaranteed to have something at least as tall. Add the water for that wall and move that pointer inward. O(n) time, O(1) space. The total can reach 1 billion, which fits in a 32-bit int.

problems.title: Pop the Pairs
problems.statement:
In `text`, whenever **two equal letters sit next to each other**, they pop and disappear. After a pair disappears, the letters on both sides may become neighbours and can pop too. Keep going until no two equal letters are adjacent.

Return the **remaining text** (it can be empty).
constraints: text contains only lowercase letters a-z

examples.explanation: bb pops, then aa pops (they became neighbours), leaving ca.
The pair pops and nothing is left.

hints.nudge: When you read a letter, which letter does it have to be compared with?
hints.pattern: Use a stack of the letters that are still there.
hints.walkthrough: Repeatedly scanning and deleting pairs can take O(n^2). With a stack, process the letters once: if the new letter equals the letter on top of the stack, they form a pair, so pop the top and skip the new letter; otherwise push it. The stack always holds the text with all pairs seen so far already removed. At the end the stack is the answer.

problems.title: Distinct in a Sorted List
problems.statement:
A librarian keeps `ids` sorted from smallest to largest, but some IDs were entered more than once.

Return **how many different IDs** the list contains.

examples.explanation: The IDs 1 and 2.
The IDs 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4.

hints.nudge: The list is sorted, so equal IDs sit side by side. When does a new ID begin?
hints.pattern: Compare each element with the previous one (a slow pointer marks the last distinct value).
hints.pseudocode:
count = 1
for i from 1 to n-1: if ids[i] != ids[i-1]: count++
return count
hints.walkthrough: You do not need a set: because the list is sorted, all copies of a value are next to each other. A new distinct value starts exactly where an element differs from the one before it. Count those starts, plus the first element. One pass, O(1) space.

problems.title: Remove From the End
problems.statement: You are given `head`, the first node of a singly linked list, and a number `n`. **Remove the `n`-th node counting from the end** of the list (the last node is the 1st from the end) and return the head of the resulting list. `n` is never larger than the length of the list. (In the examples the list is shown as the list of its values.)

examples.explanation: The 2nd node from the end is 4, so it is removed.
Removing the only node leaves an empty list.

hints.nudge: If you knew the length, you would know which node to remove. Can you find the right spot in a single pass?
hints.pattern: Two pointers with a gap of n nodes between them.
hints.pseudocode:
dummy = node before head; fast = dummy; slow = dummy
move fast n steps forward
while fast.next: fast = fast.next; slow = slow.next
slow.next = slow.next.next
return dummy.next
hints.walkthrough: Counting the length first and then walking works in two passes. For one pass, start two pointers at a dummy node placed before the head. Move the fast pointer n steps ahead. Now move both pointers together until fast is at the last node: slow then stands right before the node to remove (the gap of n keeps it n nodes behind). Link slow past the removed node. The dummy node makes removing the head work without a special case.

problems.title: Reverse in Groups
problems.statement:
You are given `head`, the first node of a singly linked list, and a number `k`. Take the nodes **`k` at a time** from the start and reverse each group of `k` nodes. If fewer than `k` nodes remain at the end, leave them as they are.

Return the head of the new list. Re-link the existing nodes (do not create a new list of values). (In the examples the list is shown as the list of its values.)

examples.explanation: Groups (1,2) and (3,4) are reversed; the last node 5 is a short group and stays.
Only the first 3 nodes form a full group.

hints.nudge: Reversing a whole list is a known trick. Can you apply it to one group at a time, and reconnect the groups?
hints.pattern: Find the group's end, reverse just that group, and stitch it to the previous group and to the next one.
hints.pseudocode:
dummy -> head; groupPrev = dummy
loop:
  kth = k nodes ahead of groupPrev; if there are fewer than k: stop
  groupNext = kth.next
  reverse the nodes between groupPrev.next and kth (the reversed group ends by pointing to groupNext)
  groupPrev.next = kth; groupPrev = the old first node of the group (now the group's tail)
hints.walkthrough: For each group, first check there are k nodes left by walking k steps ahead (if not, stop and leave the rest untouched). Then reverse the group in place, but start the reversal with 'previous' = the node after the group, so the reversed group's last node automatically points to the rest of the list. Finally connect the node before the group to the group's new first node (the old kth node) and move on: the old first node of the group is now its tail and becomes the 'node before the next group'. A dummy node in front of the head removes special cases. O(n) time, O(1) space.

problems.title: Reverse a Linked List
problems.statement:
You are given `head`, the first node of a **singly linked list** (each node has a `val` and a `next` pointing to the following node; the last node's `next` is empty). An empty list is passed as an empty `head`.

Reverse the list and return the **new head**. (In the examples the list is shown as the list of its values.)

examples.explanation: The order of the nodes is reversed.
An empty list stays empty.

hints.nudge: Each node's 'next' pointer has to point backwards instead of forwards. What do you need to remember so you do not lose the rest of the list?
hints.pattern: Walk the list with three pointers: previous, current, next.
hints.pseudocode:
prev = null; cur = head
while cur:
  nxt = cur.next
  cur.next = prev
  prev = cur; cur = nxt
return prev
hints.walkthrough: Copying the values into an array and rebuilding works but uses O(n) extra space. Instead reverse the links in place: before changing cur.next, save the next node, then point cur.next at the previous node and move both pointers forward. When cur becomes empty, prev is the old last node, which is the new head. O(n) time, O(1) space.

problems.title: Rope Join
problems.statement:
You have several ropes with lengths `ropes[i]`. Joining two ropes into one costs the **sum of their lengths**, and the new rope can be joined again later. Repeat until only one rope is left.

Return the **smallest total cost** to join all the ropes into one. If there is only one rope, the cost is `0`.

examples.explanation: Nothing to join.

hints.nudge: Every time two ropes are joined, their lengths get paid again in all later joins that include the new rope. Which ropes should be joined first?
hints.pattern: Greedy with a min-heap: always join the two shortest ropes.
hints.pseudocode:
heap = all ropes (min-heap); total = 0
while size(heap) > 1:
  a = pop(); b = pop()
  total += a + b
  push(a + b)
return total
hints.walkthrough: A rope that is joined early is paid for again each time the resulting rope is joined later, so short ropes should be combined first and long ropes last. At each step take the two shortest ropes, pay their sum, and put the new rope back. You need quick access to the smallest items repeatedly, which is exactly a min-heap: O(log n) per push or pop and n - 1 joins, so O(n log n). The total can be a few hundred million, which still fits in a 32-bit int for n up to 50,000.

problems.title: Rotate Right
problems.statement:
A carousel has seats holding the numbers in `nums`. When it turns once, every number moves one seat to the right, and the last number wraps around to the first seat.

Return the list after the carousel turns `k` times. `k` can be larger than the length of the list.

examples.explanation: The last 3 numbers move to the front.
Two turns move 3 and 99 to the front.

hints.nudge: Turning n times (the list length) brings everything back. So how many turns really matter?
hints.pattern: Use k mod n, then reverse parts of the list.
hints.pseudocode:
k = k % n
reverse the whole list
reverse the first k elements
reverse the remaining n - k elements
hints.walkthrough: Doing k single turns costs O(n*k), far too slow for k up to a billion. First reduce k to k % n, since n turns change nothing. Then the answer is the last k elements followed by the first n - k elements. In place, you can get this with three reversals: reverse everything, then reverse the first k, then reverse the rest. O(n) time, O(1) extra space.

problems.title: Spreading Rot
problems.statement:
A crate is a grid. In `grid`, `0` is an empty cell, `1` is a **fresh** orange and `2` is a **rotten** orange. Every minute, each fresh orange that is **directly next to** (up, down, left or right) a rotten orange becomes rotten.

Return the **number of minutes** until no fresh orange is left. If some fresh orange can never rot, return `-1`. If there are no fresh oranges at the start, the answer is `0`.
constraints: 1 <= rows, cols <= 10 (every row has the same length)

examples.explanation: The rot spreads outward from the top-left corner and reaches the last orange after 4 minutes.
The orange in the bottom-left corner is cut off by empty cells.

hints.nudge: All rotten oranges start spreading at the same time. In what order do the fresh oranges rot?
hints.pattern: Multi-source breadth-first search: start the queue with ALL rotten oranges and spread level by level.
hints.pseudocode:
queue = all rotten cells (time 0); fresh = number of fresh oranges
while queue: cell, t = pop front
  for each neighbour that is fresh: make it rotten; fresh--; push (neighbour, t + 1); minutes = t + 1
return minutes if fresh == 0 else -1
hints.walkthrough: Simulating minute by minute and scanning the whole grid each minute works but is slow for big grids. A breadth-first search from all rotten oranges at once visits cells in the order they rot: level 1 is the fresh neighbours of the rotten ones (rot at minute 1), level 2 their neighbours, and so on. Count the fresh oranges at the start and decrease the count whenever one rots. The last level reached is the answer; if some fresh oranges are never reached (fresh > 0 at the end), return -1.

problems.title: Are the Trees Identical
problems.statement:
You are given `first` and `second`, the roots of two binary trees. Two trees are **identical** if they have exactly the same shape and every pair of matching nodes holds the same value.

Return `true` if the trees are identical, otherwise `false`. (In the examples a tree is written level by level from the top; `null` marks a missing child.)
constraints: 0 <= number of nodes in each tree <= 10000

examples.explanation: Same shape and values.
The 2 is a left child in one tree and a right child in the other.

hints.nudge: Two trees are the same if their roots match AND their left subtrees match AND their right subtrees match.
hints.pattern: Recursion that compares both trees at the same time.
hints.walkthrough: Compare the two trees node by node. If both nodes are missing, that part matches. If only one is missing, the shapes differ, so the answer is false. If both exist, their values must be equal and both the left subtrees and the right subtrees must be identical, which is the same question on smaller trees. Each node pair is compared once: O(n).

problems.title: Find in a Rotated List
problems.statement:
A list of **different** numbers was sorted from smallest to largest and then **rotated**: it was cut at some position and the two parts were swapped, so `[0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7]` can become `[4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2]`. (It may also be left unrotated.)

Return the **index** of `target` in `nums`, or `-1` if it is not there.
constraints: nums is a sorted list that was rotated by some amount

examples.explanation: 0 is at index 4.
3 is not in the list.

hints.nudge: In a rotated sorted list, when you cut at the middle, at least one half is still properly sorted. Which one?
hints.pattern: Binary search where you first decide which half is sorted, then check whether the target lies in that half.
hints.pseudocode:
lo = 0; hi = n-1
while lo <= hi:
  mid = (lo + hi) / 2; if nums[mid] == target: return mid
  if nums[lo] <= nums[mid]:   // left half sorted
    if nums[lo] <= target < nums[mid]: hi = mid - 1 else: lo = mid + 1
  else:                       // right half sorted
    if nums[mid] < target <= nums[hi]: lo = mid + 1 else: hi = mid - 1
return -1
hints.walkthrough: A linear scan is O(n). To keep O(log n), notice that after splitting at mid, one of the two halves has no rotation point inside it, so it is plainly sorted: you can tell which by comparing nums[lo] with nums[mid]. Check whether the target falls inside the range of the sorted half. If it does, search that half; if it does not, it can only be in the other half. Repeat. Each step halves the range.

problems.title: Find in a Sorted List
problems.statement: `nums` is sorted from smallest to largest and all its values are **different**. Return the **index** of `target` in `nums`, or `-1` if `target` is not in the list.
constraints: -1000000000 <= nums[i], target <= 1000000000, all nums different and sorted ascending

examples.explanation: 9 is at index 4.
2 is not in the list.

hints.nudge: After looking at the middle element, how many elements can you rule out?
hints.pattern: Classic binary search.
hints.pseudocode:
lo = 0; hi = n - 1
while lo <= hi:
  mid = (lo + hi) / 2
  if nums[mid] == target: return mid
  if nums[mid] < target: lo = mid + 1 else: hi = mid - 1
return -1
hints.walkthrough: Checking every element is O(n). Because the list is sorted, compare the middle element with the target: if it is equal you are done, if it is smaller the target can only be to the right, otherwise to the left. Each step halves the search range, so O(log n). Take care with the loop condition (lo <= hi) so a one-element range is still examined.

problems.title: Second Highest
problems.statement:
A quiz had several rounds, and `scores[i]` is the score of round `i`. The runner-up score is the **second highest distinct score**.

Return the runner-up score. If there are fewer than two distinct scores, return `-1`.

examples.explanation: The distinct scores are 9, 7, 5, 3. The second highest is 7.
Only one distinct score exists.

hints.nudge: You only ever need to remember the two best different values you have seen so far.
hints.pattern: Single pass keeping 'highest' and 'second highest' variables.
hints.pseudocode:
first = -1; second = -1
for each x:
  if x > first: second = first; first = x
  else if x < first and x > second: second = x
return second
hints.walkthrough: Sorting the distinct values works but costs O(n log n). One pass is enough: keep first and second, both starting at -1 (scores are never negative). A new value above first pushes the old first down to second. A value strictly between second and first becomes the new second. Equal values change nothing, which handles duplicates. If second is still -1 at the end, there was no runner-up.

problems.title: Shortest Maze Path
problems.statement:
A maze is a grid where `0` is an open cell and `1` is a wall. You start at the top-left cell and want to reach the bottom-right cell. In one move you can step **up, down, left or right** into an open cell (never into a wall, never outside the grid).

Return the **fewest moves** needed. If it is impossible (including when the start or the end is a wall), return `-1`. If the grid is a single open cell, the answer is `0`.
constraints: 1 <= rows, cols <= 100 (every row has the same length)

examples.explanation: Right, right, down, down.
Both neighbours of the start are walls.

hints.nudge: All moves cost the same. If you explore outward from the start one step at a time, when will you first reach each cell?
hints.pattern: Breadth-first search (BFS) on the grid.
hints.pseudocode:
if start or end is a wall: return -1
queue = [(0, 0)]; dist[0][0] = 0
while queue not empty:
  (r, c) = pop front
  if (r, c) is the end: return dist[r][c]
  for each open unvisited neighbour: dist[nr][nc] = dist[r][c] + 1; push it
return -1
hints.walkthrough: Trying every path (depth-first with backtracking) is exponential. Because every move costs 1, a breadth-first search visits cells in order of distance from the start: first all cells 1 move away, then 2 moves away, and so on. So the first time BFS reaches the end cell, that distance is the minimum. Use a queue, a visited marker (or distance table) so no cell is queued twice, and check the four neighbours. If the queue empties without reaching the end, return -1. O(rows * cols) time.

problems.title: Palindrome Front Patch
problems.statement:
You may add letters **only to the front** of `text`. What is the **fewest letters** you must add so that the result becomes a palindrome (reads the same forwards and backwards)?

Return that number. A text that is already a palindrome needs `0`.
constraints: text contains only lowercase letters a-z

examples.explanation: Add one a in front to get aaacecaaa.
Add dcb in front to get dcbabcd.

hints.nudge: If the first k letters already form a palindrome, you only need to mirror the other n - k letters. Which k do you want?
hints.pattern: Find the longest palindrome that starts at index 0 (a palindromic prefix). KMP's failure function finds it in linear time.
hints.pseudocode:
s = text + '#' + reverse(text)
compute the prefix function of s
longest = last value of the prefix function
return len(text) - longest
hints.walkthrough: Whatever you prepend is the reverse of the part of the text after some palindromic prefix. So you want the LONGEST palindromic prefix: the answer is n minus its length. Testing every prefix costs O(n^2). Trick: build s = text + '#' + reverse(text). A prefix of text that equals a suffix of reverse(text) is exactly a palindromic prefix of text. The KMP prefix (failure) function of s, at its last position, gives the longest such prefix in O(n).

problems.title: Skip Neighbours
problems.statement:
A street has several stalls in a row, and stall `i` gives a prize worth `prizes[i]` coins. A rule says you may **not take prizes from two stalls that are next to each other**.

Return the **most coins** you can collect.

examples.explanation: Take stalls 0, 2 and 4: 2 + 9 + 1 = 12.
Take the two 5s at the ends.

hints.nudge: Look at the last stall. If you take it, what can you say about the stall before it? If you skip it?
hints.pattern: Dynamic programming over the stalls: best(i) depends only on best(i-1) and best(i-2).
hints.pseudocode:
prev2 = 0; prev1 = 0
for each p in prizes:
  current = max(prev1, prev2 + p)
  prev2 = prev1; prev1 = current
return prev1
hints.walkthrough: Let best(i) be the most coins using the first i stalls. For stall i you either skip it (best(i-1)) or take it, which forces you to skip stall i-1, giving prizes[i] + best(i-2). So best(i) = max(best(i-1), best(i-2) + prizes[i]). Trying every legal set of stalls by recursion is exponential. Because best(i) only needs the previous two values, you can keep just two variables: O(n) time, O(1) space.

problems.title: Smallest Gap
problems.statement:
A race has several runners, and `finish_times[i]` is the finishing time of runner `i`.

Return the **smallest difference** between the finishing times of any two different runners. If two runners tied, the answer is `0`.

examples.explanation: Sorted: 4, 6, 9, 15. The closest pair is 4 and 6.
Two runners finished at time 10.

hints.nudge: Look at the first example: the closest pair ended up next to each other once the times were in order. Is that a coincidence?
hints.pattern: Sort first, then only compare neighbours.
hints.pseudocode:
sort(finish_times)
best = infinity
for i from 1 to n-1: best = min(best, finish_times[i] - finish_times[i-1])
return best
hints.walkthrough: Comparing every pair is O(n^2). After sorting, the two closest values must be adjacent: if some value sat between them, it would be even closer to one of them. So sort (O(n log n)), then scan once comparing each element with the previous one and keep the minimum difference. Total O(n log n).

problems.title: Sort a Linked List
problems.statement:
You are given `head`, the first node of a singly linked list (values in any order). Sort the list from **smallest to largest** and return the head of the sorted list. (In the examples the list is shown as the list of its values.)

Aim for `O(n log n)` time. A linked list has no random access, so think about which sorting method suits it.

examples.explanation: Sorted ascending.
Negative values sort before positive ones.

hints.nudge: Merging two sorted lists is easy and fast for linked lists. How can you split a list into two halves?
hints.pattern: Merge sort: split with slow/fast pointers, sort both halves recursively, merge them.
hints.walkthrough: Quick sort and heap sort rely on jumping to arbitrary positions, which a linked list does not allow. Merge sort fits well: find the middle node with slow and fast pointers, cut the list there, sort each half recursively, then merge the two sorted halves by splicing nodes (the same merge as for two sorted lists). Recursion depth is O(log n) and the total time is O(n log n).

problems.title: Sorted Pair Sum
problems.statement:
You are given `scores` sorted from smallest to largest (duplicates allowed) and a number `target`.

Return `true` if there are two **different positions** `i != j` with `scores[i] + scores[j] == target`, otherwise `false`.
constraints: -1000000000 <= scores[i] <= 1000000000 and scores is sorted in non-decreasing order

examples.explanation: There is only one 1, and a position cannot be used twice.

hints.nudge: The list is sorted. If the smallest and largest values add up to too much, which one should you drop?
hints.pattern: Two pointers, one at each end, moving inward.
hints.pseudocode:
i = 0; j = len-1
while i < j:
  s = scores[i] + scores[j]
  if s == target: return true
  if s < target: i++ else: j--
return false
hints.walkthrough: Trying every pair is O(n^2). Because the list is sorted, put one pointer at the smallest value and one at the largest. If their sum is too small, the left value can never reach the target with any remaining partner, so move i right. If the sum is too large, the right value is too big for every remaining partner, so move j left. Each step discards one position, so it is O(n) time with O(1) space.

problems.title: Sorted Squares
problems.statement: `nums` is sorted from smallest to largest and may contain negative numbers. Square every number, then return the squares **sorted from smallest to largest**.

examples.explanation: The squares are 16, 1, 0, 9, 100; sorted: 0, 1, 9, 16, 100.
Squares sorted.

hints.nudge: The largest square is always at one of the two ends of the list. Which end?
hints.pattern: Two pointers from both ends, filling the answer from the back.
hints.pseudocode:
i = 0; j = n-1
for pos from n-1 down to 0:
  if |nums[i]| > |nums[j]|: result[pos] = nums[i]^2; i++
  else: result[pos] = nums[j]^2; j--
hints.walkthrough: Squaring and sorting works in O(n log n). But the input is already sorted, so the biggest absolute values are at the two ends (a large negative on the left or a large positive on the right). Compare the absolute values at both ends, put the bigger square at the END of the result, and move that pointer inward. Repeat until the pointers cross. O(n) time.

problems.title: Stair Ways
problems.statement:
A robot must climb a staircase with `n` steps. In one move it can climb **1, 2 or 3 steps**. Different orders of moves count as different ways (climbing 1 then 2 is different from 2 then 1).

Return the number of distinct ways the robot can reach exactly step `n`.

examples.explanation: The last move was 1, 2 or 3 steps, so ways(4) = ways(3) + ways(2) + ways(1) = 4 + 2 + 1.

hints.nudge: Think about the robot's very last move. What step could it have been on just before that?
hints.pattern: Recursion with overlapping subproblems: ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2) + ways(n-3). Remember the answers you have already computed (memoization or a loop).
hints.pseudocode:
a = ways(0) = 1; b = ways(-1) = 0; c = ways(-2) = 0
repeat n times: (a, b, c) = (a + b + c, a, b)
return a
hints.walkthrough: The last move was 1, 2 or 3 steps, so ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2) + ways(n-3), with ways(0) = 1 and ways(negative) = 0. Writing this directly as recursion recomputes the same values again and again and takes exponential time (too slow for n = 30). Fix it by storing results in a table (memoization), or compute upward from 0 to n keeping only the last three values: O(n) time, O(1) space.

problems.title: Subarray Sum Count
problems.statement:
A sensor produced the readings in `readings` (they can be negative). A **window** is any non-empty run of consecutive readings.

Count how many windows add up to exactly `target`. Windows at different positions count separately, even if they contain the same numbers.

examples.explanation: The windows [1, 2] and [3] both add up to 3.
Every one of the 6 windows sums to 0.

hints.nudge: A window's sum is the difference of two running totals. If you know the running total now, which earlier running total would make the window equal the target?
hints.pattern: Prefix sums stored in a hash map of counts.
hints.pseudocode:
seen = {0: 1}; running = 0; count = 0
for each x:
  running += x
  count += seen.get(running - target, 0)
  seen[running] = seen.get(running, 0) + 1
return count
hints.walkthrough: Trying every start and end is O(n^2). Let running be the sum of the first i readings. A window from j+1 to i has sum running(i) - running(j). It equals the target exactly when running(j) = running(i) - target. So keep a map from each running total to how many times it appeared (starting with 0 appearing once, for windows that begin at the start) and add the count for running - target at every step. O(n) time and space. The answer can be up to about 1.25 billion, which still fits in a 32-bit int.

problems.title: Subset Sum Count
problems.statement:
A chef has `weights`, the weights of several ingredients (all positive). A **selection** is any choice of ingredients, picked by position, so two ingredients with the same weight at different positions are different choices. The empty selection is allowed.

Count how many selections have a total weight of exactly `target`.

examples.explanation: The selections are {5}, {1, 4} and {2, 3}.
Either ingredient alone works, and they are counted separately.

hints.nudge: For each ingredient you have exactly two choices. What does each choice do to the remaining target?
hints.pattern: Backtracking: take it or leave it, recursing on the rest, and stop early when you can no longer succeed.
hints.pseudocode:
count(i, remaining):
  if remaining < 0: return 0
  if i == n: return 1 if remaining == 0 else 0
  return count(i + 1, remaining - weights[i]) + count(i + 1, remaining)

answer = count(0, target)
hints.walkthrough: Every selection is a yes/no decision per ingredient, so there are 2^n selections. You can write a recursive function count(i, remaining): if i is past the last ingredient, the selection is valid only if remaining is exactly 0. Otherwise add the ways when you take ingredient i (remaining - weights[i]) and the ways when you skip it. Because all weights are positive, you can prune: once remaining goes below 0, stop. With n up to 15 this is fast enough (at most 32768 selections).

problems.title: Zero-Sum Triples
problems.statement:
Find all groups of **three numbers from `nums` that add up to 0**. Two groups are the same if they contain the same three values (the order does not matter), so `[-1, 0, 1]` and `[1, 0, -1]` count once. Each number in the list can be used at most once per group (by position).

Return the **number of different groups** (counted by their values).

examples.explanation: The groups are {-1, -1, 2} and {-1, 0, 1}.
Only the value group {0, 0, 0}, however many zeros there are.

hints.nudge: Fix the smallest number of the group. Then the other two must add up to its negative, and the rest of the list is sorted...
hints.pattern: Sort, fix one number, then use two pointers for the other two. Skip repeated values.
hints.pseudocode:
sort(nums); count = 0
for i in 0..n-3:
  if i > 0 and nums[i] == nums[i-1]: continue
  lo = i+1; hi = n-1
  while lo < hi:
    s = nums[i] + nums[lo] + nums[hi]
    if s < 0: lo++ elif s > 0: hi--
    else: count++; lo++; hi--; skip equal values on both sides
hints.walkthrough: Three nested loops are O(n^3). After sorting, fix the first value nums[i]; the other two must sum to -nums[i], which is a sorted pair-sum problem: move lo right when the sum is too small and hi left when it is too big. To count each value group once, skip a position if it equals the previous value at the same level (for i, and for lo/hi after finding a match). O(n^2) overall.

problems.title: Most Frequent Values
problems.statement:
Given the list `nums`, find the **`k` values that appear most often**.

Return them as a list ordered from the **most frequent to the least frequent**. If two values appear the same number of times, the **smaller value comes first**. `k` is never larger than the number of different values in `nums`.
constraints: 1 <= k <= number of different values in nums

examples.explanation: 1 appears 3 times, 2 appears twice, 3 once.
4 and 5 both appear twice; the smaller value 4 comes first.

hints.nudge: First count how often every value appears. Then you need the k best (count, value) pairs.
hints.pattern: Hash map of counts, then a min-heap of size k over (count, value) pairs.
hints.pseudocode:
counts = frequency map
heap = min-heap ordered by (count, -value)
for each (value, count): push; if size > k: pop the smallest
result = heap contents sorted best first
hints.walkthrough: Count the values with a hash map: O(n). Sorting all distinct values by (count descending, value ascending) and taking k works in O(d log d). A heap of size k does O(d log k): keep the k best pairs, where 'worse' means smaller count, or equal count with a larger value, so the heap's smallest element (the worst of the best k) is the one to drop. At the end sort the k survivors from best to worst.

problems.title: Sum of the Top Scores
problems.statement:
A game keeps every player's score in `scores` (repeats allowed, each entry counts). The prize pool is the **sum of the `k` highest scores**.

Return that sum.

examples.explanation: The two highest are 5 and 4.
The highest score is -1.

hints.nudge: You never need all scores in order, only the best k. Which of the best k is the weakest?
hints.pattern: A min-heap holding at most k scores.
hints.pseudocode:
heap = empty min-heap
for each score: push it; if size > k: pop the smallest
return sum of the heap
hints.walkthrough: Sorting the whole list costs O(n log n). A min-heap of size k does better when k is small: push each score and, whenever the heap holds more than k scores, remove the smallest. The scores left are exactly the k largest. Add them up. Each heap operation costs O(log k).

problems.title: Find the Town Judge
constraints: each pair [a, b] has a != b, 1 <= a, b <= n, and no pair appears twice

examples.explanation: Persons 1 and 2 trust 3, and 3 trusts nobody.
Person 3 trusts person 1, so 3 cannot be the judge.

hints.nudge: Think of 'a trusts b' as an arrow from a to b. What do the arrows look like around the judge?
hints.pattern: Count incoming and outgoing arrows for every person (in-degree and out-degree).
hints.pseudocode:
score = array of n+1 zeros
for each [a, b]: score[a]--; score[b]++
for person 1..n: if score[person] == n - 1: return person
return -1
hints.walkthrough: The judge has n - 1 arrows pointing at them and none leaving. Give each person a score: +1 for every person who trusts them, -1 for every person they trust. The judge's score is exactly n - 1, and nobody else can reach that (anyone who trusts somebody loses at least a point). One pass over the trust list fills the scores, a second pass over the people finds the judge. O(n + m).

problems.title: Longest Path in a Tree
problems.statement:
The **diameter** of a binary tree is the length of the longest path between **any two nodes**, measured in **edges** (the connections between parent and child). The path may or may not pass through the root.

Given `root`, return the diameter. A tree with zero or one node has diameter 0. (In the examples a tree is written level by level from the top; `null` marks a missing child.)

examples.explanation: The path 4 -> 2 -> 1 -> 3 has 3 edges (so does 5 -> 2 -> 1 -> 3).
One edge.

hints.nudge: The longest path has a highest node. Through that node, how long is the path in terms of its two subtrees?
hints.pattern: One recursive pass that returns each node's height while updating a global best.
hints.pseudocode:
best = 0
height(node): if node is empty: return 0
  l = height(node.left); r = height(node.right)
  best = max(best, l + r)
  return 1 + max(l, r)
hints.walkthrough: For a node, the longest path that bends at that node goes down the deepest path on the left and the deepest path on the right, so its length in edges is (left height) + (right height), with heights counted in nodes. Computing the heights separately for every node costs O(n^2). Instead compute each node's height once in a post-order recursion, and while doing so update the best answer with l + r. The height returned to the parent is 1 + max(l, r). O(n) time.

problems.title: Widest Fence
problems.statement:
A farmer has posts of different heights standing in a row, `heights[i]` being the height of post `i`. He stretches a banner between two different posts `i < j`. The banner can only be as tall as the shorter post, so the banner's area is `min(heights[i], heights[j]) * (j - i)`.

Return the **largest banner area** he can get.

examples.explanation: Posts 1 and 4: min(9, 5) * 3 = 15.
The only pair: min(4, 4) * 1 = 4.

hints.nudge: Start with the two posts farthest apart. Which post should you give up on if you want a better banner?
hints.pattern: Two pointers from both ends, always moving the shorter post inward.
hints.pseudocode:
i = 0; j = n-1; best = 0
while i < j:
  best = max(best, min(h[i], h[j]) * (j - i))
  if h[i] < h[j]: i++ else: j--
return best
hints.walkthrough: Trying every pair is O(n^2). Start with the widest banner (first and last post). The height is limited by the shorter post, so keeping that short post and moving the other pointer inward can only make the banner narrower without raising its height limit. The only move that can help is discarding the shorter post. So move the pointer at the shorter post inward, record the best area at each step, and stop when the pointers meet. O(n) time, O(1) space. The area can reach 1 billion, which still fits in a 32-bit int.

problems.title: Wildcard Match
problems.statement:
A **pattern** can contain lowercase letters and two wildcards:

- `?` matches **any single letter**,
- `*` matches **any sequence of letters**, including an empty sequence.

The pattern must match the **whole** `text`, not just a part of it. Return `true` if `pattern` matches `text`, otherwise `false`. Either string may be empty.
constraints: text contains only lowercase letters; pattern contains lowercase letters, ? and *

examples.explanation: The pattern covers only one letter.
The first * matches the empty string, a matches a, the second * matches dce, and b matches b.

hints.nudge: Look at the last character of the pattern. What are the cases: letter, ?, or *?
hints.pattern: Dynamic programming on prefixes: match(i, j) = does the first i letters of text match the first j pattern characters?
hints.pseudocode:
match(0, 0) = true; match(0, j) = match(0, j-1) if pattern[j-1] == '*' else false
match(i, j):
  if pattern[j-1] == '*': match(i, j-1) or match(i-1, j)      // * matches nothing, or one more letter
  else: match(i-1, j-1) and (pattern[j-1] == '?' or pattern[j-1] == text[i-1])
hints.walkthrough: A `*` makes plain recursion branch a lot, so remember the results for each pair (i, j): match(i, j) says whether the first i text letters match the first j pattern characters. For an ordinary letter or `?`, the last characters must fit and the earlier parts must match: match(i-1, j-1). For `*`, either it matches nothing (match(i, j-1)) or it swallows one more text letter (match(i-1, j)). The base cases: two empty prefixes match, and an empty text matches only a run of `*`. A table of (n + 1) * (m + 1) booleans gives O(n * m).

problems.title: Sum of Window Peaks
problems.statement:
A thermometer recorded `temps[i]` each hour. For every **window of `k` hours in a row**, take the **highest temperature** in that window.

Return the **sum of those highest temperatures** over all windows.

examples.explanation: The window maxima are 3, 3, 5, 5, 6, 7, which add up to 29.
With k = 1 every window is one hour: 4 + 2.

hints.nudge: When a new hour enters the window, which earlier hours can never be the maximum again?
hints.pattern: Monotonic deque of indices whose values decrease from front to back.
hints.pseudocode:
deque of indices; total = 0
for i in 0..n-1:
  while deque not empty and temps[back] <= temps[i]: pop back
  push i
  if front <= i - k: pop front
  if i >= k - 1: total += temps[front]
hints.walkthrough: Scanning every window for its maximum costs O(n*k). Keep a deque of indices in the current window whose temperatures are in decreasing order. A new value removes all smaller-or-equal values from the back (they can never be a window maximum again, because the new value is both larger and later). Remove the front if it has slid out of the window. The front always holds the index of the window maximum. Each index enters and leaves the deque once: O(n).

problems.title: Word Pattern
problems.statement:
A `pattern` is a string of lowercase letters, and a `sentence` is words separated by single spaces. The sentence **follows the pattern** if you can give every pattern letter its own word so that replacing each letter by its word produces the sentence, and **different letters get different words**.

Return `true` if the sentence follows the pattern, otherwise `false`. If the pattern and the sentence have different numbers of items, the answer is `false`.
constraints: sentence is lowercase words separated by exactly one space (no leading or trailing space)

examples.explanation: a = dog, b = cat.
a and b would both be dog, but different letters need different words.

hints.nudge: The matching has to work in both directions: letter to word and word to letter.
hints.pattern: Two hash maps (or one map checked both ways).
hints.pseudocode:
words = sentence.split(' '); if len(words) != len(pattern): return false
letterToWord = {}; wordToLetter = {}
for each i: if letterToWord has pattern[i] and it differs from words[i]: return false
  if wordToLetter has words[i] and it differs from pattern[i]: return false
  record both
return true
hints.walkthrough: Split the sentence into words; if the counts differ, the answer is false. Remember which word each letter stands for, and which letter each word stands for. For every position, the letter must map to the same word as before (if it has one), and the word must map back to the same letter as before. A one-way map is not enough: 'ab' with 'dog dog' would wrongly pass. O(n) time.
